content: Have you ever wondered why a lemon tastes so sour, while baking soda tastes bitter and feels soapy? Think about it!
If you had to group all the foods in your kitchen into two teams based on their taste, how would you do it? What makes them different?

content.title: The Taste Detectives
content.description: Animation showing a tongue tasting a lemon, zooming into the sour molecules, and then tasting baking soda, zooming into bitter molecules.

content: The sour substances contain Acids. The word 'acid' comes from the Latin word 'acere' which means sour. Bitter, soapy substances are Bases.

question: Which of the following contains an acid?

content: Look around your house and try to find 3 more things that might be acidic and 3 that might be basic based on their taste or feel.
Fun fact: Our own stomach uses an acid to digest food! The properties of acids and bases are connected to many natural processes.
Not all acids are dangerous! The acids in our food (like citric acid in lemons) are weak and safe to eat. Strong acids used in chemistry labs are the dangerous ones.
Imagine you have two identical glasses of clear liquid. One is water, and the other is a dangerous acid. How can you tell which is which without tasting it?
Is there a way to make the liquid 'reveal' its true identity using colors?

content.title: The Color Changing Magic
content.description: Animation showing drops of a mysterious juice falling into an acid and turning red, then falling into a base and turning blue.

content: We use special substances called Indicators. They change their color when added to a solution containing an acidic or a basic substance. Example: Litmus, extracted from lichens.

question: What color does blue litmus paper turn when dipped in an acid?

content: Think about a time you accidentally spilled turmeric (haldi) curry on your white shirt and washed it with soap. Did the yellow stain suddenly change its color?
Turmeric is a natural indicator! Soap is basic, so turmeric turns red when it comes in contact with soap. Science is everywhere!
Create your own turmeric paper at home by applying turmeric paste on a paper and drying it. Test it with soap solution and see the magic!
What happens when an unstoppable force (a strong acid) meets an immovable object (a strong base)? Do they explode?
If acids and bases are opposites, what happens if we mix equal amounts of them together? Who wins the battle?

content.title: The Neutralization Battle
content.description: Animation showing red acid particles and blue base particles colliding and turning into harmless white salt crystals and water droplets.

content: They cancel each other out in a process called Neutralization. The reaction between an acid and a base produces a new substance called Salt, and water. Heat is also released.

question: What are the products of a neutralization reaction?

content: The salt we eat every day (Sodium Chloride) is formed by the neutralization of Hydrochloric acid and Sodium hydroxide! It's amazing how two powerful chemicals combine to make something we eat daily.
This exact concept of neutralization is used by doctors to cure acidity in our stomachs.
A common mistake is thinking all salts are neutral. Depending on the strength of the acid and base used, a salt can be slightly acidic, basic, or neutral!
Why does your grandmother give you baking soda or an antacid when your stomach hurts after eating too much spicy food?
If our stomach has too much acid (acidity), what type of substance should we put inside to 'cancel' it out?

content.title: Calming the Acid Fire
content.description: Animation showing an irritated stomach full of red acid. A blue antacid pill enters, neutralizes the acid, and the stomach smiles.

content: We use Antacids (like Milk of Magnesia) which are mild bases to neutralize the excess acid in the stomach. Similarly, when an ant bites, it injects formic acid into the skin, which we can neutralize by rubbing moist baking soda (a base).

question: What kind of substance should be applied to an ant bite to reduce the burning sensation?

content: Imagine you are a farmer and your soil is too acidic for crops to grow. What will you add to the soil?
Farmers add quicklime (calcium oxide) which is a base, to neutralize acidic soils! Science solves real-world problems.
Nature loves balance. Whenever there is too much acid, we use a base. Whenever there is too much base, we use an acid. This is the universal rule of neutralization.
